title: Alcohol Withdrawal
scenario: A 52-year-old male is admitted to the medical unit after being found confused at home. His partner reports he stopped drinking abruptly two days ago after decades of heavy daily alcohol use.

lines: 52-year-old male admitted for altered mental status. Partner states client drinks a fifth of liquor daily and abruptly stopped 2 days ago. Client is anxious, diaphoretic, and reports feeling shaky. Bilateral hand tremors noted. Reports nausea. Alert but easily startled; oriented to person and place, not to time. Denies visual or tactile hallucinations at this time.
IV access established. CIWA-Ar protocol initiated. Labs drawn. Client resting in bed with side rails up x2, call light in reach. Fall-risk precautions in place.

Lorazepam administered per CIWA-Ar protocol for worsening tremor and anxiety. Thiamine and IV fluids infusing. Client reports seeing bugs on the bedsheet; reoriented calmly. Environment kept quiet with low lighting.
Tremors diminished. Client oriented x3. Diaphoresis resolved. Denies hallucinations. CIWA-Ar score down from 18 to 7. Resting comfortably.
Thiamine 100 mg IV before any dextrose-containing fluids
IV fluids: normal saline at 100 mL/hr
Replace magnesium and potassium per protocol

children.subject: Mental Health
children.stem: Which 4 findings are consistent with alcohol withdrawal and require follow-up?
children.rationale: Tremor, diaphoresis, tachycardia, and hypertension reflect the autonomic hyperactivity of alcohol withdrawal. Normal oxygenation, glucose, and partial orientation are not withdrawal warning cues.

children.subject: Mental Health
children.stem: For each finding, click to specify whether it reflects autonomic hyperactivity, a nutritional deficiency, or both. Each finding may reflect more than one.

rows.text: Confusion with elevated AST and chronic alcohol use

children.rationale: Tachycardia, hypertension, sweating, and tremor are autonomic hyperactivity. Low magnesium reflects nutritional depletion. Confusion in a chronic drinker can stem from both withdrawal and thiamine/nutrient deficiency.

children.subject: Mental Health
children.stem: Complete the sentence. The nurse determines that the priority concern is {1}, and the priority nursing goal is to {2}.

choices.text: prevent injury and control withdrawal severity

children.rationale: Severe alcohol withdrawal carries a high risk of seizures and delirium tremens, so preventing injury and controlling withdrawal severity take priority over lower-acuity concerns.

children.subject: Mental Health
children.stem: For each intervention, click to specify whether it is indicated or contraindicated for this client.

rows.text: Apply wrist restraints as the first-line measure
Withhold benzodiazepines to allow natural detox

children.rationale: Benzodiazepines, thiamine before glucose, and a calm environment are standard withdrawal care. Restraints as a first measure and withholding benzodiazepines increase seizure and injury risk and are contraindicated.

children.subject: Mental Health
children.stem: The client's CIWA-Ar score has risen and he now reports seeing bugs on the sheet. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keep the room quiet with low lighting
Confront the client that the bugs are not real
Encourage the client to ambulate independently

children.rationale: Escalating withdrawal is treated with protocol benzodiazepines, calm reorientation, a low-stimulation environment, and seizure precautions. Confronting hallucinations and unsupervised ambulation increase agitation and fall risk.

children.subject: Mental Health
children.stem: Which findings indicate the treatment has been effective? Select all that apply.
children.rationale: A falling CIWA-Ar score, normalizing vital signs, restored orientation, and resolved diaphoresis show withdrawal is improving. New hallucinations or rising blood pressure would indicate worsening.
